newsitem.title: UK: British petrol retail pain to continue - analysts.
newsitem.headline: British petrol retail pain to continue - analysts.

text.p: A ferocious dog-fight for Britain's petrol market, sparked about a year ago by Esso's Price Watch campaign, will continue to undermine retail margins for some time to come, analysts said on Wednesday.

"Retail margins have been diabolical since Esso launched its Price Watch campaign and we don't think they will bounce back for some time to come," said Liz Horne, business development manager at Wood Mackenzie Consultants in Edinburgh.

Horne was speaking after French oil giant Elf said it was merging its British refining and retail operations with Chevron's Gulf Oil and Murco Petroleum in a $5 billion deal aimed at easing intense pressure on downstream margins.

The link-up will give the new company about eight percent of the 22 million tonnes market with 1,500 service stations, placing it fourth in the league of petrol retailers behind Esso, Shell and British Petroleum.
But over sixty companies are still marketing gasoline in the U.K. and the process of rationalisation is just beginning, said Peter Bogin of Cambridge Energy Research Associates in Paris.

Unleaded gasoline on the Rotterdam spot market has jumped over 25 percent since this time last year while, according to a report by vehicle fleet management company PHH Vehicle Management Services, due to be published shortly, British pump prices have risen by only 12 percent.
PHH's Brecon Quaddy said retail prices were starting to rise after many months of stagnation due to intense competition among the oil majors and supermarket chains.
"There's a growing feeling that the price war has had its effect in shaking out a lot of smaller independent operators," he said.
Over 3,000 petrol stations have closed in the past year, reducing the total to below 16,000, Quaddy added.
Other analysts saw few signs of relief and said the Elf merger would have only a tiny impact on the U.K.'s gasoline surplus of around 5 million tonnes per year.
"This one transaction will not lead us to alter our view of margins," said CERA's Bogin.
"Every oil company in Europe has got to cut costs because the margins at the pumps and the refineries are still way too low," he added.

WoodMac's Horne said Elf's move, which foresees the end of crude processing at Gulf's 115,000 barrels per day refinery in Pembroke, was a step in the right direction but the sector was still in for a rough ride.

Petroleum Economics Ltd's Steve Terry told an industry conference last week that recent heavy investment in catalytic cracking capacity, unexpected increases in light crude supply and rising diesel sales were combining to produce excess gasoline.
"The surplus of gasoline is likely to continue for some time," he said.
